newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian Q4 inflation data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian Q4 inflation data.

text.p: Australian inflation came in at 0.2 percent in the December quarter to be 1.5 percent higher over 1996, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.

Median forecasts had centred on a 0.3 percent quarterly rise for an annual rate of 1.6 percent. The key underlying rate rose 0.4 percent in the quarter to be 2.1 percent higher over 1996, exactly in line with median market forecasts.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follows.
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, SOCIETE GENERALE:

"They're good figures. I think they were pretty factored into the market, the market hasn't responded very strongly at this point. They're certainly figures that I think leave the government's new forecasts of 2.0 percent on the underlying and 1.0 percent on the headline for the year ended June 30, on track. I do think there is room for a (rate) cut ... on price grounds, I think there's probably room also on activity, but I'm not expecting it next week."
NIGEL STAPLEDON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, WESTPAC:

"They were pretty much in line with expectations, the key one being the 0.4 (percent) on underlying inflation. It will confirm the forecasts released yesterday by the Treasury. Indeed, we expect underlying inflation year-to-June to be a fraction lower than 2.0 percent, so that's pretty much in line with that. The 0.2 (percent) confirms that headline inflation is heading to around 1.0 percent year-to-June."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"The figure is a shade better than market expectations, although we were 0.2 points below the market so it was a shade above our expectations. It adds to expectations of a further rate cut. We would expect that the Reserve Bank would not move in February but rather it will wait for another month to assess the initial effect of the two most recent reductions and the outcome of the living wage case."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"Very much as expected. The more important underlying inflation rate has come down to 2.1 percent, just confirming Australia's low inflation status. I would expect that underlying inflation rate to remain below 2.5 percent for the next 12 to 18 months at least. It's a good figure that had already been factored into the market. It should maintain that positive bias in short-term rates, and it's just seeing a little bit of weakness in the currency as well."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"We've got yet another round of good low inflation numbers. There are are a couple of technical reasons also why underlying inflation is probably even a little better than what we found out today. I suspect that they (the RBA) won't (cut rates) next week. I suspect that given that they have cut three times and given that there is still some effects of that to come through, they're entitled to rest on their oars a little while. What you can say from today's figure is that inflation isn't going to stand in the way of a further easing."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:
"The figures are pleasing. They were in line with our forecasts. I think it emphasises the fact that Australia is a low inflation country and increases the possibility of a further rate cut."
IVAN COLHOUN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"The market had obviously discounted such a figure because it hasn't rallied very strongly. Car prices fell a bit more than we expected this quarter and we expect them to be weak again next quarter, and also recreational goods have been very low. Apart from that it's pretty much as people expected with a big drop in mortgage interest charges holding down the headline rate."
SUSAN CREIGHTON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ABN AMRO HOARE GOVETT:

"They're very very good ... spot on market expectations. In terms of what what they mean for policy I don't think these numbers by themselves are going to bring about an interest rate cut next week. Inflation certainly won't be any hurdle to another interest rate cut, but I think the bank (RBA) will want to see wage developments ... and on the back of the confirmation of the government's expectations that growth is going to reach 3.5 percent this year ... The Bank may feel that it can just wait a little longer."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
